sections.html:
Petersburg is an independent city about 21 miles south of Richmond, on the Appomattox River, with 33,458 residents at the 2020 census. With no county government above it, the city handles everything itself: the City Assessor values property, the Commissioner of the Revenue and the Treasurer deal with other taxes, and a city code office enforces building rules. The assessor's office keeps records on roughly 15,000 parcels.

Old buildings and former industrial property are common here, which is why the vacant building and rehabilitation rules further down apply to more owners than you might expect.

sections.h2: Who to call about real estate tax
sections.html:
Three city offices share the job, and each question has a different home.

QuestionOfficePhone
Wrong assessment on a real estate billCity Assessor804-733-2333
Tax amount and whether it is paidTreasurer, City Hall, 135 N. Union St.804-733-2322
Current or delinquent balance, DMV stopBilling and Collections, 144 N. Sycamore St.804-733-2346
Elderly and veterans tax reliefCommissioner of the Revenue804-733-2317

You can pay online, in person at the Fiscal Management Office at 144 N. Sycamore Street, at a drop box at that address, or by mail to P.O. Box 1271, Petersburg, VA 23804. Credit cards carry a 3 percent convenience fee. Electronic checks carry none.

Real estate tax is billed quarterly, with installments due September 30, December 31, March 30 and June 30. The Land Book ties it together: values are set as of January 1, take effect July 1, and cover billing from that July 1 through the next June 30. The city lists a rate of $1.22 per $100 of assessed value, and City Council sets it each year, so look at your own bill for the rate that applies to you.

  • September 30: first installment.
  • December 31: second installment.
  • March 30: third installment.
  • June 30: final installment.

Before you close, ask Billing and Collections for a payoff that includes any late charges.

Reassessment happens every two years as of January 1. In a reassessment year, Change of Assessment Notices go out on January 28 to owners whose value changed. The assessor reviews every assessment in that cycle even if not all of them move.

Appraisers work by assessment neighborhood with mass appraisal methods and three approaches: sales comparison, income and cost. They study recent sales first and may set aside sales that are not arm's-length, such as family transfers, foreclosures, bank sales, estate sales and other distressed sales linked to court orders or divorces. A deeply discounted sale of an inherited house may therefore carry little weight in the neighbors' values.

New construction and renovations are added when substantially complete and billed in a supplement for the part of the year after they were finished.

There are three steps: an office review with the City Assessor, then the Board of Equalization, then the Circuit Court.

  • Office review: the application is due March 1 of the assessment year, or within 30 days of the date on the change notice.
  • Board of Equalization: appeals are due April 1 of the assessment year, or within 60 days of the notice date. The board has three members, owners with real estate backgrounds appointed by the circuit court judge.
  • Circuit Court: for owners unhappy with the board or who missed the earlier deadlines. There is no city form, and an attorney typically files it.

Call and talk to an appraiser before you file. The review is a good time to check the square footage and features on record for your house. If the assessor sends a request for income and expense data on a property and you ignore it, that data can be barred from evidence later. Under Va. Code 58.1-3379 the board starts from a presumption that the assessor is correct, so bring comparable sales, photos and repair bids.

Petersburg offers a rehabilitation credit, a damage abatement and a land use program, and it requires registration of long-vacant buildings.

  • Rehabilitation credit: improvements are exempt from added tax for five years. File before work starts, with fees of $125 for residential and $250 for commercial property.
  • Damage abatement: available if a building was unfit for use for 30 days or more and the loss cut its value by $500 or more. Apply within six months of the damage.
  • Land use: initial and annual applications are due May 1, with a $500 fee.

Sec. 22-140 of the city code requires the owner of a building vacant for 12 months or more to register it with the building code official. The annual fee is $100, and the owner must describe how the building will be maintained and show a rodent abatement plan. Check a vacant house against this rule before you sell.

The tax comes out of the sale proceeds, because Virginia ranks the real estate tax lien ahead of every other lien until it is paid. Va. Code 58.1-3340 requires the purchaser, or the trustee in a foreclosure, to apply proceeds to taxes and levies, which include penalties and interest, and it leaves the seller's share to the contract.

Va. Code 58.1-802 adds a grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 of value on the deed. The seller normally pays it.

Owners with back taxes, a vacant house, repairs they cannot fund or an inherited home often look at a direct sale. The closing agent still needs a payoff from the city, so call Billing and Collections before you sign a contract.

Work through the city offices in a sensible order. Ask the Treasurer whether each installment is paid, then ask Billing and Collections for the current balance with late charges. If the house is empty, confirm with the code office whether the vacant building registry applies. Last, give the written payoff to your title company so the lien is cleared when the deed is recorded.

  • Bring the parcel number or street address to every call.
  • Check your reassessment notice if one arrived on January 28.
  • Ask about rehabilitation credit rules before any repair work, since the application has to come first.

faqs.q: How often does Petersburg reassess real estate?
faqs.a: Every two years, as of January 1. Change of Assessment Notices are mailed January 28 of a reassessment year to owners whose value changed.

faqs.q: What are Petersburg's real estate tax due dates?
faqs.a: Installments are due September 30, December 31, March 30 and June 30.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Petersburg assessment?
faqs.a: An office review is due by March 1 of the assessment year or within 30 days of the notice. A Board of Equalization appeal is due by April 1 or within 60 days of the notice.

faqs.q: Do I have to register a vacant house in Petersburg?
faqs.a: Yes, if the building has been continuously vacant for 12 months or more. The annual registry fee is $100.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Petersburg house with unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance is paid from the proceeds at closing. Ask Billing and Collections at 804-733-2346 for a payoff before you set a closing date.
